utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. At the last sitting of the Chamber, the Defence made an oral motion requesting a postponement of the matter to the 15th of September. The Trial Chamber indicated then that the application would be dealt with in due course. We will deal with it now. Before this last motion, the Defence had made a motion, again, asking that the matter be postponed to enable the Defence to prepare itself in this matter. Therefore, this application that was made or this motion that was made orally at the last sitting was actually a repetition of a prior motion. Now, for a motion to be brought again on the same facts -- I beg your pardon. For the Chamber to be asked to reconsider its decisions on a motion that came before, it is important for new facts to be put on the table for the Chamber to consider. What Mr. Milovancevic told the Chamber at the last time was that he was now acting in that motion on the express instructions of Mr. Martic. The Chamber does not regard that as a new fact. The Defence is at all times acting on the instructions of Mr. Martic. So even the previous motion was made on his instructions. Otherwise, it was out of court. The Court wants just to remind the Defence that, in fact, previous indulgences have been given to the Defence, and also to remind the Defence that preparation in the view of the Chamber does not start at the close of the Prosecution case, but it starts at the time the Defence receives instructions from your client. So it cannot be said at this stage that witnesses are now going to be sought and be interviewed to be able to meet the Prosecution case. Indeed, the Defence has been cross-examining witnesses of the Prosecution, it must be understood that this is based on instructions from both their own client and their own witnesses. For these reasons, the Chamber feels that and rules that the application for a postponement be and is hereby dismissed. What now remains is to give an oral decision on the 98 bis submissions. This will be read very slowly so as to enable the interpreters to interpret. 1: The Trial Chamber today delivers its judgement on the Defence oral submissions on the 26th of June 2006 for a judgement of acquittal. The Defence moved for a full acquittal. The Prosecution responded the same day and opposed the Defence submissions in their entirety. 2: Pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules, the Trial Chamber shall enter by oral decision and after having heard the parties' oral submissions, a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. It is important to note that the rule was amended in 2004 and now focuses on counts rather than as before charges. The Defence did not make submissions on the standard to be applied pursuant to Rule 98 bis. However, the Defence submitted that, "The Prosecution has to prove Mr. Martic's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in this stage of the proceedings." Furthermore, on several occasions, the Defence made allegations of crimes committed by other parties to the conflict. The Defence also made extensive argument on the credibility of Prosecution witnesses. In light of these submissions the Trial Chamber finds it necessary to address the applicable standard pursuant to Rule 98 bis. 3: The standard to be applied in respect of each count of the indictment is whether the evidence, if believed, that is taken at its highest, could lead a reasonable trier of fact to convict the accused on the respective count. This standard does not imply an assessment of the alleged guilt of Mr. Milan Martic in light of the evidence adduced during the Prosecution's case. This judgement therefore does not entail considering the credibility of the Prosecution's witnesses or weighing the evidence. Significantly, the Trial Chamber's assessment does not involve an evaluation of the strength or weakness of contradictory or different evidence before the Trial Chamber. 4: The Defence's submissions in these respects are therefore dismissed as falling outside the scope of Rule 98 bis. 5: The Trial Chamber in the Mrksic case recently rendered its oral judgement pursuant to Rule 98 bis. That Trial Chamber held that the rule in its new incarnation, "Does not also require evidence capable of establishing each and every allegation or form of liability, that is criminal responsibility pleaded in respect of a count to support a conviction on a count." The Mrksic Trial Chamber held that while there must be evidence which meets the standard in respect of every element of the offence alleged by the count, "This may be established even though the evidence is not necessarily sufficient in respect of some other allegations or particulars set out in the indictment in respect of that encounter or in respect of one or some forms of criminal responsibility relied on by the Prosecution." This Trial Chamber is of the same opinion and furthermore agrees with the Mrksic Trial Chamber that, "The Prosecution need only ultimately succeed in proving one of the forms of criminal responsibility it relies on for there to be a conviction on a count." The Trial Chamber will therefore consider the submissions of the parties on the basis of the above observations regarding the applicable standard pursuant to Rule 98 bis. In doing so, it makes an evaluation of all the evidence on the trial record. 6: The indictment against Mr. Milan Martic focuses on the period from August 1991 until 31 December 1995 when he held various positions within the SAO Krajina, later called the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK. It is a matter of agreed facts between the parties that the SAO Krajina was established on the 21st of December 1990. There is evidence that throughout 1991, Territorial Defence, the TO, and the police of the SAO Krajina, together with the Yugoslav national army, the JNA, engaged in armed conflict with the Croatian Territorial Defence, the Croatian police and the Croatian National Guard in the territory of the SAO Krajina, including in places such as Pakrac, Plitvice, and Kijevo. Approximately one year later, that is on the 19th of December, the assembly of the SAO Krajina in Knin proclaimed the Republic of Serb Krajina, the RSK. This is also an agreed fact. There were numerous cease-fire agreements and agreements regarding the withdrawal of the JNA from the -- from Croatia in 1991. The Vance Plan, which was eventually signed by Slobodan Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman provided for United Nations Protected Areas or UNPAs, demilitarisation of the Krajina and maintaining the peace and security to allow for the return of refugees of all ethnicities. However, the Vance Plan was not properly implemented in the SAO Krajina and the cease-fire was regularly violated. Mr. Milan Martic's positions as Minister of the Interior, minister of the Defence and deputy commander of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina are established by the agreed facts and are not subject to dispute. Mr. Milan Martic held at least the positions of Minister of the Interior, and deputy commander of Territorial Defence also during the existence of the RSK. It is also an agreed fact that on the 25th of January 1994, Milan Martic was elected president of the RSK. In respect of the above, the Trial Chamber refers to the testimony of Veljko Dzakula, Reynaud Theunens, Charles Kirudja and Peter Galbraith. 7: Mr. Milan Martic is charged with all modes of liability pursuant to Article 7(1) of the statute in relation to each count in the indictment, in particular with participating in a joint criminal enterprise in its basic and extended forms. Mr. Milan Martic is also charged with superior responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for each count in the indictment. 8: The common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise is alleged as the forcible removal of a majority of the Croat, Muslim and other non-Serb population from approximately one-third of the territory of Croatia and large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in order to make those areas part of a new Serb-dominated state. It is alleged that this common purpose was furthered by the commission of the crimes alleged in the 19 counts of the indictment, that is violations of the lawyers or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and crimes against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute. In the alternative, it is alleged that the crimes pleaded in the indictment with the exception of the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise and that Milan Martic was aware of these crimes. This is the extended form of the joint criminal enterprise. It is alleged that Mr. Milan Martic and numerous other persons participated in the joint criminal enterprise by contributing significantly to its common purpose. 9: The Defence has submitted that no evidence has been adduced to show that there was an oral or a written plan of the joint criminal enterprise. However, according to the consistent jurisprudence of the Tribunal since the Tadic appeals judgement in 1999 the existence of a common purpose need not have been previously arranged or formulated. Accordingly, the Prosecution is not required to prove the existence of an explicit agreement or a formal plan. Indeed, the common purpose may materialise extemporaneously and may be inferred from the fact that a plurality of persons act in unison to put into effect a joint criminal enterprise. Nevertheless, according to the Appeals Chamber in Krnojelac -- I'm sorry, I can't pronounce his name properly, in Krnojelac this element has to be identified as precisely as possible and when it is inferred from circumstantial evidence, the inference must be the only available inference available on that evidence. As will be shown in the following, the Trial Chamber's view is that the evidence properly satisfies this standard. 10: There is evidence that idea of creating a new state which would include Serbs from all the former republics of Yugoslavia was initially envisaged by Serb authorities in Belgrade, notably Slobodan Milosevic and Borislav Jovic and was then endorsed in Croatia by the SAO Krajina leadership including Milan Martic. The evidence shows that Milan Martic told witness MM-079 during a visit to Knin in May 1991 that, "The Serbs of Krajina wanted to live in one single country with all the other Serbs from Yugoslavia, including Serbia, and that by no means would the Serb people live under the Ustasha authorities in Croatia." In this respect, the Chamber refers to the following evidence as illustrative. Peter Galbraith at 3746 to 47; Witness MM-079 at 3069 to 71; and Charles Kirudja at 4838 to 39. 11: The evidence shows that Milan Martic in his positions in the SAO Krajina and RSK closely cooperated with the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade. In relation to the alleged responsibility under Article 7(3), there is evidence that Milan Martic had effective control over the police and the TO of the SAO Krajina and the SVK. Milan Martic throughout the period of the indictment was in close contact with officers of the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade, in particular Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic. Numerous meetings were also held by Milan Martic with these officers, both in Belgrade and in Knin. The Trial Chamber has received considerable evidence which shows that the Ministry of Interior in Belgrade provided financial, logistical and military assistance to the SAO Krajina and Milan Martic. A particularly notable example is the training camp in Golubic, just north of Knin, which was set up in 1991 by Milan Martic with the assistance of Dragan Vasiljkovic and Frenki Simatovic. There is evidence that the government of the SAO Krajina formed special police units under the Ministry of the Interior, then under the control of Milan Martic. There is considerable evidence that these special police units were trained at the Golubic camp. There is also evidence to show that these forces of the Ministry of the Interior participated in important operations such as Operation Corridor for the purpose of taking control of "territories under Croatian or the Bosnia and Herzegovinian units and authorities and to establish a direct communication with Serbia by road." Moreover, these units were also active in Bosanski Novi. The existence of close cooperation between Milan Martic and the authorities in Belgrade is further supported by evidence of reports containing operational information on the situation in the SAO Krajina which were regularly sent to the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade. Some relevant evidence in this respect is that of Reynaud Theunens at 703 and 797. Witness MM-003 at 1982, 1982 to 95, 1987 to 89 -- I beg your pardon, 87 to 88, 2003, 2041, 2134, 2212 to 213; Marko Miljanic at 2959; Peter Galbraith at 3756 to 57. Rade Raseta at 3921 to 22; Witness MM-078 at 4539 and 4547, Exhibits 38, 39, 469, 537, 698 and 707. 12: There is also evidence that Milan Martic and other Serb leaders of the SAO Krajina and of the RSK worked in close cooperation with leaders of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ARK. Hamdija Krupic testified that on the agendas of the meetings in the ARK municipalities were the establishment of so-called Serb municipalities which were to be joined up with the SAO Krajina in order to form a single territory. Veljko Dzakula testified that what mattered to Milan Martic in sessions of the RSK was "to work for recognition in joining the association of Serb lands, Republika Srpska and Serbia." The Chamber refers to Hamdija Krupic at 2943 and Veljko Dzakula at 404 to 405. 13: Inference as to the existence of a common purpose may also be drawn from the cooperation of military units and civilian authorities in conducting armed operations within the territory of the SAO Krajina and the RSK. Milan Martic himself recognised on more than one occasion the good cooperation and coordination between the army and the police. There is evidence of a joint assignment for linking up all Serb lands into one single territory and that coordination meetings were held with leaders of military units and police units to be engaged in join combat operations. Specifically, there is evidence that Milan Martic participated in two such meetings with the 9th corps and that where he was not present, members of the Ministry of the Interior would report back to him. Reference is made here inter alia to witness MM-078 at 4412 and 4442 and Exhibit 518; Witness MM-003 at 2022 to 23; Radoslav Maksic at 1165 to 69, and Exhibit 692. 14: There is evidence which allows for the reasonable inference that Milan Martic shared intent with the principal perpetrators of the crimes committed in furthering of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. The evidence supports the conclusion that Milan Martic backed the displacement of the non-Serb population from the areas indicated in the indictment. In relation to the Red Cross's planned return of displaced victims of the Skabrnja attack, Milan Martic in a letter to the UNPROFOR command in Zagreb dated the 28th of September 1992, stated that, "We will be forced to prevent an arrival by force -- I beg your pardon, on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Similar inferences can be drawn from evidence which shows that Milan Martic talked of the takeover of villages such as Kijevo, Saborsko and Skabrnja as a victory against the Croats. For instance, Milan Martic stated that the mission in Skabrnja was, "To cleanse it from the Croat population." And he describes Saborsko as, "Pure Serb land." Moreover, Milan Martic is described as having, "Shared the goal of the army and the police to join up the Serb lands and cleanse the Croat areas that were in the way of Croat civilians and all Croats." The evidence indicates that Milan Martic would often visit places where fighting occurred in order to boost the people's morale. In relation to the attack on Skabrnja on the 18th of November 1991, Milan Martic stated that Goran Opacic, who was a member of the Benkovac police and therefore part of the Ministry of Interior under Martic had done the job well and had completed the mission. Relevant evidence in this respect includes Dzakula at 404 to 405, Witness MM-003 at 2024 to 25, 2026 [sic], 2190, and Witness MM-079 at 3112 to 113. 15: There is considerable evidence that persons of non-Serb ethnicity in the territory of the SAO Krajina/RSK and in Bosanski Novi/Bosanska Kostajnica were exposed to severe forms of terror, violence, and discriminatory treatment during the indictment period. The evidence indicates that the objective of inter alia the special police units was to terrorise the local non-Serb population and make them leave the territory. This reached such levels as to make their further stay in these territories impossible. The record shows that as a result of this coercion, a very large number of persons left their homes and were bussed out in convoys, then organised manner by the relevant Serb authorities in the territories of both the SAO Krajina and Bosanski Novi/Bosanska Kostajnica. The Trial Chamber notes that there appears to have been coordination between the authorities of the SAO Krajina, RSK, and the ARK. While the resulting displacement may have been described as voluntary in official documents of the Serb authorities, the evidence allows the conclusion that the continued threat and intimidation was of such a level and character that the non-Serb population did not have a genuine choice to remain. There is evidence that Milan Martic knew of and even encouraged through speeches in the media, the displacement of the non-Serb population from the territory of the SAO Krajina. The Trial Chamber notes the evidence of Witness MM-003, at 2190 to 91, John McElligott at 4595 to 96, Charles Kirudja at INS, Witness MM-078 at 4461, 4468, 4518 to 19, 4521, 4588 to 89, and 4595 to 96, as well as the several UNCIVPOL documents in evidence. The Trial Chamber finds that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on counts 10 and 11. 16: There is evidence that beginning in 1991, attacks were launched on numerous Croat villages within the territory of the SAO Krajina. These attacks appear to have followed the same general pattern. Police of the SAO Krajina and RSK directly participated in the attacks, together with units of the JNA and the TO. The purpose of the attacks was to remove the non-Serb population from the attacked areas. Civilians were killed, detained, driven out or made to flee. There was general destruction of dwellings and religious buildings in the areas which were torched, shelled or otherwise destroyed. There is also evidence that plunder and looting was carried out by the attacking forces. Evidence relation to the attacks and killings, plunder and destruction of property includes the evidence of Aernout van Lynden, Ana Bicanic, Ana Kesic, Ante Marinovic, Anton Blazevic, Bosko Brkic, Jasna Denona, Josip Josipovic, Jure Vukovic, Luka Brkic, Marica Vukovic, Marko Miljanic, Marko Vukovic, Mijo Cipric, Neven Segaric, Tomislav Kozarcanin, Tomislav Segaric, Vlado Vukovic, Witness MM-003, Witness MM-022, Witness MM-036, Witness MM-037, Witness MM-038, Witness MM-078, Witness MM-083, Exhibit 507. The Trial Chamber finds that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on counts 2 to 4 and 12 to 14. 17: There is evidence that persons of non-Serb ethnicity were detained in various detention facilities throughout the SAO Krajina and RSK. This included the prison in Knin, the old hospital in Knin, also known as Martic's prison, and that at the Tova-Korenica police station. At these locations detainees were subjected to acts of physical and mental violence which may properly be described as torture, cruel treatment, and inhumane acts. The Trial Chamber refers in particular to the evidence of Luka Brkic at 3226 to 27, 3266, 3268 to 73, 3279 to 85, 3439, and Mladen Loncar at 5435, Witness MM-079 at 3099, 3102 to 03, Vlado Vukovic at 2524 to 25, 2670 to 71, Stanko Erstic in Exhibit 397, and Exhibit 392. And the Trial Chamber finds that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on counts 5 to 9. 18: In relation to counts 15 to 19, which alleges responsibility for the shelling of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May 1995, there is evidence that Milan Martic ordered the shelling on both dates using the Orkan rocket launcher system. Evidence in this respect comes from witnesses MM-003, at 2043 to 44 and Exhibits 97, 98, and 388. There is also evidence that these shelling incidents resulted in a large number of civilian fatalities and casualties. Evidence in this respect includes Branko Lazarevic, Sanja Bintic at 5647 to 5674, Mina Zunac at 5819 to 5822, Vaseljka Gromoja at 5781, Ivan Mikulcic at 5598 to 5599, Sanja Risovic at 5582 to 5584 and Exhibits 388, 799, and 802, and the Trial Chamber finds that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on counts 15 to 19. 19: Count 1 of the indictment charges Milan Martic with individual criminal responsibility for persecutions under Article 5(A) of the statute. As the Trial Chamber has found that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on the other counts, the Trial Chamber concludes that this is true also of count 1. 20: There is evidence to conclude that the joint criminal enterprise on both its basic and extended forms have been proven for the purposes of Rule 98 bis. The Trial Chamber therefore concludes that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Martic on all counts of the indictment. 21: And just to sum up, there is therefore no basis on which the Trial Chamber can enter a judgement of acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 bis. I'm sorry, Judge Nosworthy has just brought to my attention that at the end of paragraph 14, where I referred to Witness MM-003, at 2024 to 25 and then I also said 2026 instead of 2062, if that correction could be made. Thank you very much. I guess this brings us to the end of the business for the day, unless there are any housekeeping matters. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to raise an issue which has to do precisely with this ruling that we just heard from the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 98 bis. It is the first time that the Defence now has before it the position of the Trial Chamber in relation to all counts of the indictment. This was this ruling made in accordance with Rule 98 bis. This is something that should guide the Defence in further proceedings. The Defence would like to point out that in their oral ruling, the Trial Chamber referred to a number of witness statements and their evidence. In the view of the Defence it is very difficult to assess such evidence when we do not have a final position in relation to the evidence of Milan Babic. The relevancy and veracity of the evidence of these witnesses that the Trial Chamber referred to is something that the Defence may not assess properly and accurately in a situation where we do not know what is the status of Milan Babic's evidence. However, despite of that, we are bound to comply with all the rulings of the Trial Chamber, including their ruling on when the Defence case is to begin. In several instances we tried to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the situation where we receive instructions from Mr. Martic, the instructions that are binding for us. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, the Defence would like to inform the Trial Chamber with the written instructions we received from Mr. Martic. We had it translated and we made sufficient copies for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. We now find ourselves a situation where we have to plan our work under the circumstances where we do not know exactly which Prosecution evidence will stand, and this is what we are facing at the beginning of the Defence case. The entire position of the Prosecution is based on the evidence of witness Milan Babic. All counts of the indictment including factual and legal issues are based on his evidence. Even though the status of this evidence is still not finally resolved, the Trial Chamber adopted this ruling. We find ourselves in a situation where the legal position is not entirely clear as to which evidence will be allowed to stand and which won't. We have to proceed working under those circumstances. Naturally, we have to comply with the ruling of the Trial Chamber. However, this leads us into the conflict of interests of the accused. By continuing working under such circumstances, or rather it would be completely illogical for us to continue working under the circumstances the Trial Chamber expects us to work; however, Mr. Martic expects us not to embark on the Defence case until -- unless we are fully prepared. We now have an entirely new legal and factual situation. The Trial Chamber has assessed the Prosecution case and even though we know which counts there are in the indictment, we do not know which evidence will be allowed to stand. Ones again, we ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider this situation and to judge the circumstances in which the Defence finds itself and they have been radically changed in relation to, say, yesterday. This is the first time that we were given an inkling of what the Trial Chamber thinks of the status of evidence so far. The Defence is expected to proceed with work contrary to the instructions of our client. This is against the interests of our client and I think that this situation can be resolved only if the Defence team is to withdraw. However, I don't think that that is an option or rather no Defence team can work against the interests of clients and contrary to the client's instructions. Our client gave us written instructions, we provided them to you, we believe that the reasons stated therein are reasonable and logical and by going contrary to the instructions of our client, we would be seriously harming his interests. We apply to the Trial Chamber to assist us in this matter. We have invested a lot of effort, this Defence team has been working for more than three years on this case, since the trial began we've been here on a daily basis for more than five months now and we believe that given the legal and factual consequences, given how serious they are, we believe that our appeal to the Trial Chamber is fully justified and we expect to encounter some understanding in relation to our situation. With your permission, I would now distribute the instructions we received from Mr. Martic. Would the usher please assist us so that we could give a copy to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... might I interrupt you before you proceed to delivery? I must confess, Mr. Milovancevic, I consider the course that you're about to embark on highly unorthodox and I have never, ever known it been adopted before. As a general rule, the Bench ought not to be privy to instructions coming from your client, because it's normally regarded as highly confidential and subject to privilege passing between attorney and client. Granted, there are circumstances where the accused may consent, but it is not usual to pass the instructions of the accused to the OTP. This, I understand, and know to be one of the hallowed rules of legal procedure and practice and it touches and concerns your duty to your client. Might I inquire of you if your client has been duly advised and counseled as to all the several consequences of the course which you are about to embark on and before that, I would like to hear from you what is the jurisprudence before this Tribunal for the course which you are now going to embark on? I would like to hear from you, Mr. Milovancevic, and after hearing from you, I would also like to hear from learned counsel for the OTP. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the manner in which the Defence communicates with a client in this case, against the accused, Mr. Martic, is via direct oral communication. During these three years, we have opted for such a way of communication whereby the Defence would come to The Hague on a monthly basis before the trial began, visit Mr. Martic for four to five days in the detention unit, and receive all instructions from him orally. This situation that you have described, Your Honour, is fully accurate. However, we find ourselves in an impossible position because, from our own client, officially, we received a motion which ties our hands in our future work. Faced with a need to make the Trial Chamber understand our position, we opted for this radical solution, which is such that we received instructions mandating that we comply with them strictly as formulated in writing. Naturally, if you believe that this is contrary to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, we will not insist on turning over this motion to you. We simply wanted to inform, fully inform, the Trial Chamber about the key problem faced by the Defence. We as a Defence team are in a very delicate situation because we can see that what our client is instructing us to do is minimal by nature and fully reasonable, fully justified in relation to the time frame imposed by the Trial Chamber. That's on the one hand. And then on the other hand, we are duty bound and we have always done this, to comply with all the rulings of the Trial Chamber, and so far we have complied with all of them. We are doing what we can now. We do not want you to view us as negligent and we also do not want you to think that we are drawing wrong conclusions from the instructions of our client. The instruction that is we received from him are not dealing with the substance of Defence case, no. These are not instructions about what needs to be done, with which piece of evidence. So in that sense we are not harming the interests of the accused or his rights, nor are we disclosing the confidential portion of our communication with him. No. These instructions are simply dealing with the future schedule and deadlines that, in view of the accused, are important, and these are instructions that he is giving to us. This is what we propose to acquaint you with, Your Honours, by giving you this motion. We were only guided by our desire to make you see the position of the Defence in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, is it a motion or is it instructions? Because I've heard you use both words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just looked at the text again. Mr. Martic uses the following words. He says that our client, he is giving instructions to us and he says that he is issuing a written order to us. I used the term instruction in the broader sense but these are -- yes, his instructions for the Defence. I failed to mention another matter, Your Honours, namely that Mr. Martic asked us to keep him informed about this and to have a fully -- to have fully open channels of communication in relation to this. Mr. Martic insisted on this. He insisted on us putting this forward. We have in no way violated the attorney-client privilege by doing so. We simply believe it to be important for the Trial Chamber and for the continuation of these proceedings to ensure that the Trial Chamber fully understands the position in which the Defence finds itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy wanted to hear the Prosecution on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm extremely grateful to the Bench for raising this issue. Our position is I think as follows: It's certainly unorthodox, though in principle there is nothing barring the Defence counsel and the accused from assenting to disclosing this material to the Trial Chamber or to the OTP. The wisdom is another matter. But I think that it would be important that before that occurs, that -- and maybe Defence counsel has already stated it but I missed it, but that it's stated clearly on the record by Defence counsel that the accused assents to this material - whatever it is; it's been described as instructions - that it -- that the accused assents to it being disclosed to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber. And that once it's disclosed it can be used in whatever manner anybody deems fit. I don't -- I take counsel at his word that it's merely about scheduling but if there is other material in there that becomes relevant in some way, then it becomes relevant. It's disclosed and I think the accused should be warned about that. And perhaps as an additional precaution -- obviously the accused is here in court but as an additional precaution perhaps the Trial Chamber could briefly inquire of the accused himself if that is correct, if he could just affirm that that -- that he has consented. I would say, if I may, while I'm on my feet just briefly, I'm not really sure how having these instructions handed up to the Trial Chamber or to the OTP advances the ball in any way. There is nothing magical about these instructions. The accused cannot simply by writing it down on a piece of paper instruct or ordering his Defence counsel, upend the schedule that the Trial Chamber has set down again and again, and it doesn't -- he can't simply stop the trial because he has ordered it. And so I don't really see how it's going to advance the ball at all to have this handed around. I would also just, if I may very briefly, say I take issue with Defence counsel's characterisation that the Trial Chamber has somehow given its view of the evidence at this stage and suddenly there has been this radical change. I don't see Rule 98 bis as being that at all. I don't think the Trial Chamber has given its view of the evidence. It's merely given its view of the 98 bis standard. There is a lot of weighing and determining and judging that has yet to be done and has not occurred. I don't think that the decision that the Trial Chamber provided today is its view of the evidence at all. I think we are operating really very much from a clean slate. We have put forward the case for the Prosecution and the evidence and now it's -- and I don't think that anything has been prejudged or the Trial Chamber has not reached any decisions or conclusions about the evidence whatsoever. So nothing really has changed today. And then, and in particular the Defence counsel keeps going back to Babic but I noted that and I may be -- I'll be corrected if I'm wrong but I don't think the Trial Chamber even relied on -- cited Mr. Babic once in its decision on 98 bis so I don't think there, there is anything -- has changed. And if I may, I think that the accused really has two options here now, that the Trial Chamber has ruled, and has set down the schedule. The accused can either start its defence or if it has no defence to put forth before the Trial Chamber, then it rests and we proceed to final argument and judgement. There really is not a third option in our submission, that we -- that the accused simply by repeatedly saying "we should stop, we should stop," that that becomes a third option. And I think really I think from our view, our point of view, the Defence is beginning to risk a contempt or sanctions from the Court for repeatedly raising this, and I would cite both Rule 77, which is the contempt rule, and also Rule 73(D), which is the rule about frivolous motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me start off by saying to you what you have raised now -- no, you may sit down. You may sit down, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm speaking. What you have raised now, this Chamber has decided before. What you have raised now, this Chamber has just decided this morning again before we started today's proceedings. You are raising one and the same issue time and time and over again, and that you raise it in different language each time does not make it substantially a different matter. It still is the same point. And I think it is important for the Defence to remember that if you do want the Chamber to reconsider its decision, you've got to bring in new facts to consider. Otherwise, if you don't bring in new facts, you are saying it was crazy to give the order it gave when it did give that order. And if you don't have new facts, then go and appeal. There are procedures here open to parties. And I just want to warn against your repeated going back to this point that we must postpone this matter. It does verge on an abuse of process and it does verge on contempt, and I just want to say also to you that it is true what the Prosecution says, that the 98 bis decision did not once refer to the evidence of Babic. Now, as to what the evidence of Babic -- what the status of the evidence of Babic is, that's a matter for the Appeals Chamber to decide. You have taken that matter on appeal. The appeal court will decide that point. That does not mean that there is no other evidence on the record that the Defence must contend with and we can proceed with the case, we can deal with the case as it stands. Obviously, if the appeal is decided in favour of the Defence, then the Defence has not been prejudiced. In fact, the Defence has been relieved of a further duty to deal with but to deal with the case as it stands now. And let me say to you that it may very well be in your own interests or in the interests of your client to advise him to appreciate that this Court, like any other court, operates on rules and procedures and that when orders are made, they are made and to be respected, and for him to say, "and I order you to do A or B," he mustn't think that that intimidates the Court. He does not. Instead, he is himself verging on contempt and I want you to tell him that. So he either wishes to carry on with the case as ordered, or he rests his case. We are not going -- this Chamber is not going to be held to ran some by an accused. We have given plentiful indulgences right through the trial where we thought they were called for. I do not think, and this Chamber does not think so, that at this point there is any merit in the application for a postponement of this matter. There is nothing to stop the appeal going on parallel with the trial going on. You will hear in due course, I suppose the appeal is going to be heard as soon as possible, and the trial must go on. Let me just say that I hope this is the last time this Chamber is seized of this application specifically to postpone before the opening of the Defence case. Just before I stop, let me see what my learned Judge wants to tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My sister on the right just reminds me to tell you something that I thought was obvious and I wasn't going to tell you, that you obviously are expected to prepare your case at the highest point. In other words, in anticipation of Mr. Babic's evidence being included. This is -- actually this is the flip side of what I mentioned, that if it doesn't -- if it does get excluded, then of course the Defence will be relieved but that's the case that you had always known you were supposed to meet from day one, so with those words, I just want to say that I hope this is the last time we have heard of this application for this postponement before the opening of the Defence case and the matter is accordingly adjourned -- I've got to find out to when -- to Friday, the 7th, for a Pre-Defence Conference, but the trial to start on the 11th, at 9.00, of July. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.08 a.m.,
